deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. This page continues fragment XXVII, 'Fragmente über die Grenzfälle der elliptischen Modulfunctionen', an Additamentum to §40 of Jacobi's Fundamenta Nova. Riemann wants the boundary values (|q| = 1) of Jacobi's q-series. Those series diverge on |q| = 1, so he first integrates them against dq/q. The previous page gave the integrated series as Lambert-type log-series (48–54). This page re-expands the same integrals in powers of q (55–61). It then states the Abelian limit lemma that justifies evaluating them on the unit circle.

NOTATION (modern). Use Jacobi's theta functions: theta3 = sum q^(n^2), theta4 = sum (-1)^n q^(n^2), theta2 = sum q^((n+1/2)^2). Then:
- 2K/pi = theta3^2,
- k = theta2^2/theta3^2 and k' = theta4^2/theta3^2,
- 2kK/pi = theta2^2, 2k'K/pi = theta4^2, 2 sqrt(k') K/pi = theta3*theta4 = theta4(q^2)^2.
In 55–57 (Jacobi's §40 notation), p runs over odd numbers and psi(p) = sigma(p), the sum of the divisors of p. All integrals are taken from 0, so a term c*q^N/N in the result corresponds to the term c*q^N in the integrand.

55) Claim: integral of log(k/(4 sqrt q)) dq/q = -4 sum_p sigma(p)/p^2 (q^p - (3/4)q^{2p} - (3/16)q^{4p} - ...). The correction coefficients are 3/4^l for l >= 1.
Equivalently (applying q d/dq, my step): log(k/(4 sqrt q)) = -4 sum_p (sigma(p)/p)(q^p - (3/2)q^{2p} - (3/4)q^{4p} - ...).
Source: k = 4 sqrt(q) prod((1+q^{2n})/(1+q^{2n-1}))^4.
My check of low coefficients: -4q + 6q^2 - (16/3)q^3 + 3q^4. This agrees with the formula.

56) Claim: integral of -log k' dq/q = 8 sum_{p odd} sigma(p) q^p/p^2.
Derivation (my step): k' = prod((1-q^{2n-1})/(1+q^{2n-1}))^4. Since log((1+x)/(1-x)) = 2 sum_{j odd} x^j/j, we get -log k' = 8 sum_{p odd} (sigma(p)/p) q^p. Integrating against dq/q divides each term by p. This is consistent with 49.

57) Claim: integral of log(2K/pi) dq/q = 4 sum_p sigma(p)/p^2 (q^p - (1/2)q^{2p} - (1/4)q^{4p} - ...).
Equivalently: log theta3^2 = 4 sum_p (sigma(p)/p)(q^p - q^{2p} - q^{4p} - ...).
My check against theta3^2 = 1 + 4q + 4q^2 + 4q^4 + ...: log = 4q - 4q^2 + (16/3)q^3 + ... . This agrees.

58)–61) NOTATION CHANGE. Here psi(n) must be read differently. My interpretation (not stated on this page, but forced by correctness):
- n runs over numbers all of whose prime factors are of the form 4k+1;
- psi(n) is the number of divisors of n;
- '(4m-1)' runs over numbers all of whose prime factors are of the form 4k-1, including 1;
- l >= 0.
Under this reading, psi(n) summed over N' = (4m-1)^2 n equals E(N') = d_1(N') - d_3(N'), the excess of divisors congruent to 1 over those congruent to 3 mod 4 (Jacobi's phi). Also r2(N) = 4E(N) for the sum-of-two-squares count.

58) theta3^2 - 1 = sum_N r2(N) q^N. Hence the integral is 4 sum_N E(N) q^N/N. Writing N = 2^l (4m-1)^2 n gives Riemann's formula.

59) theta2^2 = 4 sum_{N odd} E(N) q^{N/2}. Hence the integral is 8 sum_{N odd} E(N) q^{N/2}/N, with N = (4m-1)^2 n.

60) theta4^2 - 1 = sum (-1)^N r2(N) q^N. The odd-N terms give the first (negative) sum; the even-N terms, N = 2^{l+1}(odd), give the second sum.

61) theta3*theta4 - 1 = theta4(q^2)^2 - 1 = sum (-1)^N 4E(N) q^{2N}. Integration gives terms q^{2N}/(2N). Odd N gives the first sum; N = 2^{l+1}(odd) gives exponents 2^{l+2}(4m-1)^2 n.

LEMMA (Latin text). If sum a_n converges in the order written, then lim_{r -> 1-} sum a_n r^n = sum a_n.
Corollary: let f(q) = sum a_n q^n for |q| < 1. If the series converges at a point q0 with |q0| = 1, its sum equals the limit of f(q) as q -> q0 radially ('ut modulus tantum mutetur'), i.e. along the normal to the boundary circle.
Purpose: on the next page this identifies the boundary values at q0 = e^{ix} of the integrated functions with the (conditionally) convergent series 62 ff. Those series involve log(4 cos^2(nx/2)) and sawtooth terms ((nx/2pi)). These are the discontinuous functions the fragment studies, and the source of Dedekind's later commentary.
errors: No mathematical errors found in 55–61 under the stated interpretation of the notation.

The notation psi is silently overloaded. In 55–57 it is Jacobi's psi(p) = sigma(p) for odd p. In 58–61 it must mean the number of divisors of n (n composed of primes 4k+1), with (4m-1) standing for any product of primes of the form 4k-1, including 1, and l >= 0. Taken literally as m = 1, 2, 3, ... (i.e. 3, 7, 11, ...), formulas 58–61 would be wrong. This is an ambiguity of notation, presumably defined elsewhere, not an error of substance.

The lemma is stated only for radial approach, which is exactly what Abel's theorem gives. Riemann correctly restricts the corollary to radial limits ('ut modulus tantum mutetur'). He does not claim the non-tangential (Stolz) extension.
Trivial: the series a_0 + a_1 + a_2 is written without trailing dots.

results.what: q-expansions of the integrals of log(k/4 sqrt q), -log k', log(2K/pi) against dq/q in terms of divisor sums sigma(p) over odd p (55–57)
results.modern_name: Logarithmic q-expansions of theta quotients / Eisenstein-type divisor-sum series (integrated)

results.what: Integrated expansions of theta3^2-1, theta2^2, theta4^2-1, theta3 theta4 - 1 with coefficients d_1(N)-d_3(N), written via the factorization N = 2^l b^2 n (58–61)
results.modern_name: Jacobi's two-squares theorem r2(N) = 4(d_1(N)-d_3(N)) and its multiplicative form

results.what: Lemma: a convergent series sum a_n gives lim_{r->1-} sum a_n r^n = sum a_n; corollary for radial boundary values of power series on |q|=1
results.usually_credited_to: N. H. Abel 1826 (Stolz 1875 for the non-tangential extension)

results.what: Programme of studying boundary values of elliptic modular functions on |q|=1 by integrating Jacobi's series (fragment XXVII)
results.modern_name: Boundary behaviour of modular forms; precursor of Dedekind sums and the eta transformation
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (fragment published by Dedekind & Weber in the Werke, 1876), with Dedekind's 1877 commentary introducing Dedekind sums

deep.surprise_reason: This page belongs to the fragment 'Fragmente über die Grenzfälle der elliptischen Modulfunctionen', printed in Riemann's Gesammelte Werke (1876) and famous as the starting point of Dedekind's 1877 commentary (Dedekind sums, eta transformation). Its content consists of routine q-expansions of Jacobi's §40 formulas plus Abel's theorem, so nothing here is new or unattributed.
